query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The tribo‐corrosion degradation rate of a CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy under sliding in chloride‐containing aqueous solution is governed by the dynamic regeneration kinetics and stability of its protective passive oxide film; boosting passive film stability (via increased Cr content) simultaneously suppresses both wear and corrosion losses.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA with a homogeneous equiaxed grain structure, polished to Ra <50 nm.
generation.intervention: Increase Cr content from 20 at.% to 25 at.% at the expense of Fe, maintaining all other elements equiatomic.
generation.conditions: Reciprocating sliding (normal load 5 N, speed 100 mm/s, stroke 5 mm) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 25 °C for 30 min.
generation.structural_mediator: Thickness, composition, and adhesion strength of the passive oxide film formed at the sliding contact interface.
generation.mechanism: Higher Cr accelerates repassivation and forms a more adherent, Cr‐rich oxide that shields fresh metal from corrosive attack and reduces direct asperity contact, lowering both electrochemical dissolution and mechanical wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the equiatomic baseline, the Cr‐enriched HEA will show ~40% lower total mass loss under tribo‐corrosion, comprising ~30% lower wear volume and ~50% lower average corrosion current density.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA under the same sliding and solution conditions.
generation.boundary: Prediction holds in chloride‐containing aqueous environments under moderate loads (<10 N) and sliding speeds (<200 mm/s); it fails under dry or inert atmospheres where passive film formation is negligible.
generation.uncertainty: Effect‐size estimates are approximate; performance at higher loads, different temperatures, or other electrolytes is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Reciprocating tribo‐electrochemical test comparing equiatomic and Cr‐enriched HEAs under identical load, speed, and 3.5 wt.% NaCl environment. Monitor mass loss, friction, and electrochemical current in situ; characterize oxide film thickness and chemistry post‐test by XPS and cross‐sectional FIB‐SEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if the Cr‐enriched HEA does not exhibit a thicker or more Cr‐rich adhesive oxide film AND does not demonstrate simultaneous reductions in both wear volume and corrosion current relative to the baseline.
